about: Sources behind the Swim Tools app's rules (docs/swim-tools-app.md). Written for members first: headline, takeaway, what it means for your workouts, how sure the evidence is, where to read more; the formal citation last. Rules in trainingMetrics.json point here by id (their `basis`). Until `reviewed.by` is filled in, the site labels an entry "Pending review"; production should hide unreviewed entries.

evidenceLabels.strong: Strong: a review of many studies, or a large, consistent body of research
evidenceLabels.moderate: Moderate: a few good studies, or a widely used coaching framework
evidenceLabels.early: Early: promising but thin or debated
evidenceLabels.usms: USMS content: written by USMS coaches

references.headline: Where the workouts come from
references.takeaway: Every set Swim Tools uses is taken from USMS's six-week freestyle training plans (50 to 1650 free), written for swimmers training without a coach on deck.
references.inYourWorkouts: Sets keep the plans' own effort words (cruise, steady, solid, strong, race), drills and equipment. Swim Tools chooses and orders them, and adjusts the number of repeats, but never invents new ones.
references.caveats: All six plans are short course yards and freestyle-focused. Other strokes and courses are converted or left out until more plans are added.

references.headline: Finding your threshold pace from two timed swims
references.takeaway: Swim two distances all-out (for example a 400 and a 200). The difference between them gives a 'critical swim speed', a good estimate of the fastest pace you can hold for a long time.
references.inYourWorkouts: When we know two of your times, threshold sets give you a target pace per 100 instead of just an effort word.
references.caveats: Tested in competitive (non-Masters) swimmers. See the next entry: the estimate runs slightly fast.

citation.authors: Wakayoshi K, Ikuta K, Yoshida T, Udo M, Moritani T, Mutoh Y, Miyashita M
citation.title: Determination and validity of critical velocity as an index of swimming performance in the competitive swimmer

references.headline: Why your threshold target is a little slower than your test says
references.takeaway: Critical swim speed came out a bit faster (about 93% of top aerobic speed) than the pace swimmers could truly hold steady (about 88%).
references.inYourWorkouts: Threshold sets aim 2–5 seconds per 100 slower than your calculated critical speed, so the set stays sustainable.
references.caveats: A small study of young competitive swimmers.

citation.authors: Dekerle J, Pelayo P, Clipet B, Depretz S, Lefevre T, Sidney M
citation.title: Critical swimming speed does not represent the speed at maximal lactate steady state

references.headline: Why sprint and distance plans feel so different
references.takeaway: Elite sprinters mix lots of easy swimming with very fast work and little in between. Distance swimmers do the most easy swimming, a good amount of moderate work and the least very hard work.
references.inYourWorkouts: A 50 or 100 free plan pairs easy aerobic days with short, fast sets. A 500 to 1650 plan spends more time at a steady, moderately hard pace.

evidence.basedOn: Systematic review of 9 studies of elite swimmers

references.caveats: Elite swimmers training far more than most Masters swimmers. We borrow the shape of the plan, not the volume.

citation.authors: González-Ravé JM, Hermosilla F, González-Mohíno F, Casado A, Pyne DB
citation.title: Training intensity distribution, training volume, and periodization models in elite swimmers: a systematic review
citation.source: International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance 16(7):913–926

references.headline: Match the training to the race
references.takeaway: Over 12 weeks, swimmers who trained the sprint way improved their 100 free the most, and those who trained the distance way improved their 800 free and aerobic capacity the most.
references.inYourWorkouts: Your plan's mix of easy, moderate and hard sessions follows the event you chose.

citation.authors: Arroyo-Toledo J, Sortwell A, Clemente-Suárez V
citation.title: The effect of 12-week of pyramidal and polarized training intensity distribution in national elite adolescent swimmers

references.headline: What 'steady', 'solid' and 'strong' mean for your body
references.takeaway: Swimming intensities fall into zones, from easy aerobic work up to all-out sprints. Each zone can be recognized by how hard it feels, your heart rate, or how your stroke holds up.
references.inYourWorkouts: Every set is tagged with a zone, so you can see whether a workout is mostly easy, mostly threshold or mostly fast.

citation.authors: Fernandes RJ, Carvalho DD, Figueiredo P
citation.title: Training zones in competitive swimming: a biophysical approach
citation.source: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living 6:1363730

references.headline: How hard was it? Your answer counts
references.takeaway: Rate a whole session from 1 to 10 and multiply by its minutes, and you get a simple, reliable measure of how much training you did.
references.inYourWorkouts: When you log a swim, you rate it 1–10. Your plan uses your ratings to decide whether the next week should be lighter or harder.

citation.authors: Foster C, Florhaug JA, Franklin J, et al.
citation.title: A new approach to monitoring exercise training
citation.source: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research 15(1):109–115

references.headline: Effort ratings work in the pool too
references.takeaway: In swimmers, session effort ratings tracked heart-rate-based training load closely. Coaches tended to underrate the hard days and overrate the easy ones compared with the swimmers.
references.inYourWorkouts: The plan trusts your rating of a session over the effort the workout prescribed.

citation.authors: Wallace LK, Slattery KM, Coutts AJ
citation.title: The ecological validity and application of the session-RPE method for quantifying training loads in swimming
citation.source: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research 23(1):33–38

references.headline: Don't ramp up too fast
references.takeaway: Sudden jumps in training compared with what you've been doing lately are linked with more injuries, but studies measure this so differently that no single number is proven.
references.inYourWorkouts: If a week would be much bigger than your recent average, the plan suggests a lighter session. It's a nudge, not a rule.

evidence.basedOn: Systematic review of 27 studies, mostly team sports

references.caveats: Mostly team sports, not swimming, and the method is debated.

citation.authors: Griffin A, Kenny IC, Comyns TM, Lyons M
citation.title: The association between the acute:chronic workload ratio and injury and its application in team sports: a systematic review

references.headline: Why your last two weeks get shorter, not easier
references.takeaway: Across many studies, cutting distance by about half over the final two weeks, while keeping the fast efforts and the number of swims, made athletes about 3% faster on race day.
references.inYourWorkouts: Plans aimed at a meet trim each session's distance in the last two weeks. Your fast sets stay fast.

evidence.basedOn: Meta-analysis of 27 studies of swimmers, runners and cyclists

references.caveats: Most participants were younger competitive athletes, not Masters swimmers.

citation.authors: Bosquet L, Montpetit J, Arvisais D, Mujika I
citation.title: Effects of tapering on performance: a meta-analysis

references.headline: Practicing your race pace in short pieces
references.takeaway: Many short swims (like 25s) at goal race pace with short rest can improve speed with less fatigue than traditional hard sets, but only a handful of studies exist.
references.inYourWorkouts: Sprint plans include an optional race-pace set based on your goal time. You can turn it off.
references.caveats: Very few studies, mostly young competitive swimmers.

readMore.label: Scoping review: does volume and interval matter?

citation.title: Intensity and pace calculation of ultra short race pace training (USRPT) in swimming: take-home messages and statements for swimming coaches

references.headline: Why every workout starts easy, then wakes up
references.takeaway: A good warm-up builds gradually and includes a few short efforts near race pace. It seems to help most for races of 200 or longer, though results vary.
references.inYourWorkouts: Every workout opens with a warm-up, and before a fast main set it includes a few short, quicker swims.

evidence.basedOn: Review of warm-up studies in competitive swimming

references.caveats: Studied before races, in competitive swimmers.

citation.authors: Neiva HP, Marques MC, Barbosa TM, Izquierdo M, Marinho DA
citation.title: Warm-up and performance in competitive swimming

references.headline: Why the plans keep asking you to count strokes
references.takeaway: Distance per stroke was the single best predictor of performance in a middle-distance freestyle swim. Efficient swimmers go farther with each stroke.
references.inYourWorkouts: Sets that say 'take one less stroke per 25' or 'same stroke count' build that efficiency. You can log your stroke count to track it.

citation.title: Energy expenditure during front crawl swimming: predicting success in middle-distance events

references.headline: Training as a Masters swimmer
references.takeaway: Masters swimming times hold up well into middle age and then slow gradually. How fast depends on the stroke, the distance and sex.
references.inYourWorkouts: Goal times are checked against real results for your age group, so targets stay realistic.
references.caveats: Based on race results, not training studies.

citation.authors: Knechtle B, Barbosa TM, Nikolaidis PT
citation.title: The age-related changes and sex difference in master swimming performance

references.headline: Predicting a time for a distance you haven't swum
references.takeaway: Across endurance sports, how much you slow down as the distance grows follows a steady pattern, so one time can predict another.
references.inYourWorkouts: If you set a goal for an event you haven't raced, your goal pace is estimated from your other swims.

evidence.basedOn: World records across running, swimming and other sports

references.caveats: Built from world-record performances. We are checking it against USMS results before relying on it.
